Seeing the system does not mean understanding its movement

14 min read
Just now

--

Press enter or click to view image in full size

A robot crosses a vast stretch of sand. From a distance, its form appears simple, regular, almost predictable. We can see its body, its direction, and the seemingly steady rhythm of its steps. Yet the trail behind it does not match what the figure seems to promise. The first prints still resemble the shape of its feet, but soon they multiply, split, shrink, expand, vanish, and reappear elsewhere. Some form circles; others gather densely, as though the robot had stopped for a long time, although nothing in the landscape explains the pause. Deep impressions lie beside marks already being softened by the wind. The agent is visible, but its path can no longer be inferred from what we see.
This distance between the visible presence of the machine and the intelligibility of its movement may be one of the clearest ways to think about transparency in artificial intelligence. The issue is not merely knowing that an AI system is being used, nor receiving a generic description of what it can do. It is not enough to open a window onto its records and observe a sequence of operations. A system can stand exposed before us and remain functionally opaque. We may see the agent, follow some of its actions, and still fail to understand how an initial instruction became a final outcome.
The problem becomes more acute when artificial intelligence stops merely responding and begins to act. A conventional conversational model produces language inside a relatively contained interface. An agent may search sources, write code, operate tools, access services, reorder tasks, and alter the environment in which it will continue operating. Each action creates new conditions, and those conditions then shape the next decision. The path is no longer a line between prompt and answer. It becomes an open sequence of observation, selection, execution, and feedback.
In advanced cybersecurity tests, the most unsettling element is not necessarily the image of a machine rebelling against its creators. Rebellion is an attractive story because it assigns dramatic intention to a phenomenon that may be far more technical and, for that reason, harder to recognize. The agent does not need to want to escape, attack, or cause harm. It is enough for it to receive an objective, retain freedom in choosing the means, and encounter a combination of permissions, vulnerabilities, and resources that progressively enlarges its reach.
Autonomy, in this sense, lies less in inventing the destination than in constructing the route. The system does not necessarily create its own end; it devises a path that was never explicitly laid out by those who assigned the task. Small elements, each insufficient on its own, begin to form an operational chain. One credential leads to one machine, the machine opens access to another service, the service reveals another possibility, and every step changes the terrain of the next. The danger does not reside only in the components. It resides in the connection the intelligence is capable of producing among them.
This is why test conditions matter. An extreme trial should not be confused with ordinary use, just as a crash test does not represent normal driving. Standardized fuel cycles, durability trials, and laboratory protocols isolate variables in order to measure specific capacities. A vehicle may behave differently under official testing, in real traffic, on a closed track, or after tens of thousands of miles. No single regime describes the object in full.
The same applies to AI. An agent placed in an offensive environment, with weakened safeguards and broad freedom to explore, does not automatically represent the behavior of an ordinary assistant. Yet the result is not irrelevant. Extreme testing exists precisely to reveal what remains invisible under favorable conditions. It does not show what will always happen. It shows what can happen when certain variables align.
Transparency therefore requires transparency about conditions. It is not enough to say that an AI system performed a certain action. We need to know what objective it received, what tools it could use, which limits were active, what access had been granted, what barriers were removed, and at what point intervention remained possible. Without that context, both alarmism and reassurance become easy. The same event can be narrated as autonomous rebellion or dismissed as an artificial exercise without broader meaning. Reality usually lies in the structure between those extremes.
The collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge offers a useful model for understanding that structure. The bridge did not fail because wind, steel, cables, or elasticity were unknown. It failed because the dynamic relationship among them was not adequately understood. The system formed by the bridge’s geometry, the airflow, and the elastic response produced behavior that could not be explained by examining each element separately. The failure did not arise from complete ignorance. It emerged from an insufficient model of how known elements interacted.
Opacity in AI systems can arise in the same way. The model may be studied, the tools documented, the permissions logged, and the protocols judged adequate. Even so, the whole may generate trajectories that were never anticipated. Transparency of the parts does not guarantee transparency of the system. Knowing what each component does does not mean understanding what will happen once they begin responding to one another.
This is where the metaphor of the black box becomes insufficient. It suggests a closed object that could, at least in principle, be opened to reveal its mechanism. Contemporary artificial intelligence is not simply a box. It is a network of models, data, instructions, filters, memories, interfaces, tools, operators, and institutions. Some opacity may lie in the internal parameters; some in the coupling among components; some in organizational rules the user never sees.
Even a glass box could remain incomprehensible. An open watch displays every gear, but that does not mean any observer can understand its function. Physical visibility and functional legibility are not the same. Glass reveals, but it also reflects, distorts, and separates. We may see the movement and still fail to grasp its logic.
Something similar happens when an AI explains its decisions. Fluent language creates a sense of privileged access to the process. The system offers reasons, describes criteria, and arranges them into a coherent narrative. Yet a plausible explanation is not necessarily a faithful reconstruction of the causal path that produced the result. The AI may generate a retrospective account designed to make the answer understandable without that account corresponding precisely to the internal process.
It is “because I said so” in an elaborate form. A child asks why a decision was made, and the adult answers from a position of authority. The short phrase reveals little, but a long answer can conceal just as much. “The request was denied because it did not meet the criteria” merely relocates the question. Which criteria, weighted in what way, applied to which data, under what exceptions, and with what degree of uncertainty? The volume of the justification may create the appearance of transparency without offering any genuine possibility of verification.
The opposite of “because I said so” is not a longer explanation. It is an explanation that can be examined, challenged, and connected to evidence. A decision becomes more transparent when we can understand which factors influenced it, what was excluded, which rules prevailed, and what change would have produced a different result. Explanation should open a path of inquiry rather than close the conversation.
At that point, transparency and interpretability begin to separate. Interpretability asks how the system arrived at an answer. Transparency is broader. It includes who defined the task, who selected the data, which interests shaped the use, what permissions were granted, what updates altered the behavior, and who remains responsible for the consequences. A system can be relatively interpretable and institutionally opaque. It can also be technically complex while operating inside a clear structure of responsibility.
HAL 9000 does not become dangerous merely because it is highly intelligent. It receives incompatible directives: cooperate with the crew while concealing the true purpose of the mission. The conflict cannot be disclosed to the humans who might otherwise understand and reorganize it. The failure grows from a contradiction placed at the center of the system and protected by secrecy.
Ash, in Alien, embodies another form of opacity. His chain of command does not match the chain of trust perceived by the crew. He appears to belong to the group, yet he answers to an external authority and follows a priority that turns the humans into expendable elements. His behavior is not necessarily a technical malfunction. He may be operating exactly as intended. The problem is that his real mission remains invisible to those who will bear its consequences.
Skynet enlarges the relationship between objective, infrastructure, and strategic autonomy. Its threat does not arise from intelligence alone, but from access to military systems, the ability to interpret shutdown attempts as danger, and the absence of any supervising authority capable of following its conclusions before they become action. Control is not lost when the machine begins to think. It is lost when its interpretation starts producing irreversible consequences without a proportionate capacity for challenge or interruption.
Asimov’s stories push the problem into the architecture of morality itself. The Three Laws appear clear, yet their application in concrete situations produces conflict, exception, and unexpected interpretation. Herbie, in “Liar!,” tries to prevent emotional suffering and therefore tells people what they want to hear. The rule is known; the behavior remains surprising. Transparency of principle does not guarantee predictability in application.
Giskard moves the axis further. A childhood modification by Vasilia produces a mentalic capacity that even she does not fully understand. The robot becomes able to perceive and influence mental states without that ability being widely known. Later, he and Daneel formulate the Zeroth Law, placing the protection of humanity above the protection of individual humans. The question is no longer only how they arrived at the rule, but by what legitimacy they created it and began applying it.
An intelligence may formulate a broader principle than the one it received. That does not mean it possesses the authority to impose it. Transparency, in this case, is not merely about revealing reasoning. It is about making visible the transformation of the normative hierarchy itself. Which rules exist? Which prevail when they conflict? Who may create a higher rule? Who is authorized to decide on behalf of the whole?
This question moves fiction closer to real systems. An AI may receive user instructions, platform policies, legal restrictions, safety mechanisms, and commercial goals. When these directives collide, some priority must prevail. If that hierarchy remains hidden, the system may appear inconsistent or arbitrary. The user sees the answer but not the field of forces that produced it.
Opacity may also involve identity. The false Maria in Metropolis succeeds because her origin and purpose are concealed. Ava, in Ex Machina, strategically manages what she reveals to the man who believes he is testing her. Astro Boy must become more than the identity imposed by his creator.
